$$
\text{I.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}\,\text{II.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡14 & (\text{mod}\,16)\end{aligned}\,\text{III.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,4) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}\,
$$

Select all that apply.
solution:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem does *not* apply to system I since $6$ and $8$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,8)=2>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system II. The numbers $3,$ and $16$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 16=48.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system III since $4$ and $12$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(4,12)=4>1
$$

So, the correct answer is "II only."

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the lowest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Which of the plots above represent symmetric relations defined on the set $A={0,2,4}?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In terms of a plot, if a point $(x,y)$ belongs to the plot, then $(y,x),$ the point symmetric to $(x,y)$ over the diagonal line $y=x,$ should also be on the plot.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

So, only one of the points, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be on the plot of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows points on the diagonal line $y=x.$

With that in mind, let's draw the diagonal line $y=x$ and examine our plots.

![](images/9c/9c9c16300cfb95a61a261e39db865d5c6d056794bd7aaa422567bde10dd4abf5.png)

 

- Plot I represents a symmetric relation since the plot is symmetric over the line $y=x.$

- Plot II represents an antisymmetric relation since the plot contains at most one point from each pair of the points symmetric over the line $y=x.$

- Plot III represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since, for example, the pair $(4,2)$ belongs to the plot while the point $(2,4)$ does not. And it's not antisymmetric since it contains the pairs $(0,4)$ and $(4,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

- Curve III is a simple and closed curve but it is not negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed counterclockwise, so it is positively oriented.

- Curve IV is not simple.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
